common_name: Aaron's Beard (Creeping St. John's Wort, Rose of Sharon Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to poor, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Aaron's beard spreads by underground rhizomes to form a dense, weed-smothering mat and tolerates the dry, root-filled soil under trees better than most flowering groundcovers.

directions: Plant in average to poor, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath trees or on a bank too difficult to mow; Aaron's beard is a low, semi-evergreen, trailing sub-shrub grown for large, bright golden-yellow flowers with a prominent burst of long stamens that open through summer over blue-green foliage. It spreads steadily by underground rhizomes into a dense, weed-suppressing mat, tolerating dry shade, root competition, and poor soil better than nearly any other flowering groundcover, which makes it a workhorse for stabilizing shaded slopes and banks where mowing is impractical. Because it spreads assertively, give it a contained space, such as a bank bordered by pavement or a bed edged with a mowing strip, rather than a small formal border where its vigor would be unwelcome. Shear old plantings back close to the ground in late winter every few years to rejuvenate growth and keep flowering strong.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in gritty, sharply drained, neutral to alkaline soil in partial shade; rose daphne resents root disturbance and wet feet above all else, so choose its permanent site — ideally a rock garden or raised bed with excellent drainage — carefully from the start.

directions: Plant in gritty, sharply drained, neutral to alkaline soil in partial shade, ideally on a slope or raised bed where water never stands around the roots; rose daphne is a low, mat-forming, evergreen shrub that in late spring smothers itself in small, intensely fragrant, rosy-pink flower clusters — one of the most powerfully scented small shrubs grown, easily perfuming an entire rock garden or path. It is a classic choice for alpine and rock gardens, where its trailing habit can drape attractively over stones. Good drainage is the single non-negotiable requirement for success; more rose daphnes are lost to wet, heavy soil than to cold, pests, or neglect. Like other daphnes, it resents being moved once established, so plant it in its permanent spot and avoid disturbing the root zone afterward. Mulch lightly with gravel rather than organic mulch to keep the crown dry.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, consistently wet, peaty soil in partial shade; bog laurel is a true bog plant native to northern peatlands and needs saturated, acidic conditions similar to its relatives leatherleaf and sheep laurel.

directions: Plant in acidic, consistently wet, peaty soil in partial shade; bog laurel is a low, wiry, evergreen shrub of northern peat bogs, with narrow leaves that are dark green above and whitish underneath, and in late spring produces clusters of small, saucer-shaped, rose-pink flowers held above the foliage on the current season's new growth. Growing naturally in permanently saturated, nutrient-poor, acidic bogs alongside sphagnum moss, it is a plant for a true bog garden or an engineered rain garden basin kept consistently wet and acidic, not an ordinary moist border — normal garden soil and drying out are both fatal to it over time. Like its relative mountain laurel, all parts of the plant contain grayanotoxins and are toxic if ingested, so keep it away from grazing animals and out of reach of children and pets. Where conditions genuinely suit it, bog laurel needs essentially no maintenance once established.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in consistently moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; climbing fetterbush grows naturally in Gulf South cypress and blackgum swamps and needs the same acidic, wet conditions in cultivation.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; climbing fetterbush is an unusual native Gulf South evergreen shrub with small, glossy, dark-green leaves and clusters of small white urn-shaped flowers similar to its relative Pieris japonica, but famous for a remarkable habit in the wild — in its native cypress and blackgum swamps, it grows as a true climber, sending stems up underneath the loose, fibrous bark of the host tree, invisible except where leafy branchlets emerge through cracks in the bark many feet up the trunk. In ordinary garden cultivation without a suitable host tree, it instead grows as a low, sprawling, spreading shrub, still worthwhile for its evergreen foliage and flowers in a wet, shaded native plant garden. It needs the same reliably moist, acidic soil as its swampy origin and struggles if allowed to dry out. A conversation-piece native shrub for a bog garden or swamp-margin planting within its narrow Gulf South range.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; tarflower is adapted to the fire-prone pine flatwoods and scrub of the Gulf South and tolerates poor, dry, sandy soil once established.

directions: Plant in acidic, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; tarflower is a native evergreen shrub of Gulf South pine flatwoods and sandy scrub, blooming in late summer with clusters of fragrant, white-to-pink, sticky flowers whose petals are edged with tiny glandular hairs that exude a resinous, tar-like substance — hence the common name, and a genuine curiosity, since bees visiting the flowers often end up with a bit of sticky residue on their bodies. It is a fire-adapted plant of longleaf pine ecosystems, resprouting vigorously after burns in the wild, and is highly drought tolerant in the deep, fast-draining sand it evolved in. Grown occasionally by native-plant nurseries for wildlife gardens and low-water landscaping within its native range, it asks for little beyond sharp drainage and lean, acidic soil; rich garden soil or poor drainage are more likely to cause problems than neglect. Its long late-summer bloom period is valuable for native pollinators when many other shrubs have finished flowering.

planting.note: Set out small starter plugs or divisions in spring into consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; panakenake spreads by creeping stems that root as they go, knitting into a solid mat within a season or two under reliable moisture.

directions: Plant divisions or starter plugs in consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; panakenake is a New Zealand native creeping groundcover forming a very low, dense carpet of small, rounded, glossy leaves, studded in summer with tiny white star-shaped flowers followed by an unusual show of small, rounded, deep magenta-purple berries that persist for weeks — a distinctive feature that sets it apart from similar low flowering groundcovers, which typically lack showy fruit. It roots as it spreads and tolerates light foot traffic once established, making it useful between shaded stepping stones or as a lawn substitute in a damp, shaded nook. Keep the soil from drying out, since it thins quickly in drought, and provide reliable shade in hot climates to keep the foliage from scorching. Divide congested patches in spring to fill bare spots or start new plantings.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown crowns in spring in deep, rich, constantly moist to boggy soil in partial shade; giant gunnera needs a genuinely wet site — the margin of a pond or stream, or a bog garden basin kept saturated — and generous room to spread its enormous leaves.

directions: Plant in deep, rich, constantly moist to boggy soil in partial shade at a pond or stream margin, giving it as much room as a large shrub since a well-grown specimen produces enormous, coarsely lobed, rhubarb-like leaves that can reach five feet or more across on thick, prickly stalks. In summer it sends up bizarre, cone-shaped flower spikes from the base, followed by small orange-brown seed clusters, but the giant foliage is the real reason it is grown — few perennials create a bolder, more tropical-looking accent at the edge of a water feature or bog garden. It needs constant moisture and rich soil to reach full size and will scorch or stall in dry conditions. In the colder part of its hardiness range, protect the dormant crown over winter with a thick mulch of its own cut-back leaves or straw, since a hard freeze reaching the crown can kill the plant outright. Site it away from small paths, since the leaf stalks are covered in stiff prickles.
